questiontext.text:
Prove that \(n^3 - n\) is a multiple of 3 for every integer \(n\).

Drag the blocks into order to make a proof by exhaustion. Use every block.

[[parsons input="ans1"]] {"steps": {# parsons_encode(proof_steps) #}, "headers": ["Your proof:"], "available_header": ["Drag from here:"]} [[/parsons]]
[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
One correct proof:

Let \(n\) be any integer. Then \(n^3 - n = (n - 1)\,n\,(n + 1)\).

Every integer is a multiple of 3, or 1 more than a multiple of 3, or 2 more than a multiple of 3. So \(n = 3k\), \(n = 3k + 1\) or \(n = 3k + 2\) for some integer \(k\).

Case \(n = 3k\). The factor \(n = 3k\) is a multiple of 3.

Case \(n = 3k + 1\). The factor \(n - 1 = 3k\) is a multiple of 3.

Case \(n = 3k + 2\). The factor \(n + 1 = 3k + 3 = 3(k + 1)\) is a multiple of 3.

In every case one of the factors of \((n - 1)\,n\,(n + 1)\) is a multiple of 3, so \(n^3 - n\) is a multiple of 3.

The three cases can come in any order: each one stands on its own. In each case a different factor of \((n - 1)\,n\,(n + 1)\) carries the 3. The same idea, with seven cases, proves that \(n^7 - n\) is a multiple of 7.
